clinicalPearls: Irregular, reddish-brown to grey linear streaks radiating from the peripapillary area beneath the retinal vessels, representing crack-like breaks in a brittle, calcified Bruch membrane

Frequently associated with systemic disease, classically pseudoxanthoma elasticum, and also with Paget disease of bone, sickle cell and other haemoglobinopathies, and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, though some cases are idiopathic
A characteristic peau d'orange mottling of the posterior pole may accompany the streaks, particularly in pseudoxanthoma elasticum
Often asymptomatic until complicated by choroidal neovascularisation, which is the main cause of central visual loss
The eyes are vulnerable to choroidal rupture and subretinal haemorrhage after even minor blunt trauma, so protective eyewear and avoidance of contact sports are advised
Fluorescein and indocyanine green angiography and optical coherence tomography help delineate the streaks and detect choroidal neovascular membranes
Fundus autofluorescence can highlight the streaks and associated retinal pigment epithelial changes
Management centres on treating secondary choroidal neovascularisation with anti-VEGF therapy and on investigating and managing the underlying systemic association
reference.pathophysiology: Angioid streaks are breaks in Bruch membrane, the elastic layer between the retinal pigment epithelium and choriocapillaris, which becomes abnormally thickened, calcified and brittle. In pseudoxanthoma elasticum and related disorders the underlying defect is degeneration and mineralisation of elastic tissue, which weakens Bruch membrane so that it cracks, producing the visible streaks. These breaks disrupt the barrier between the choroid and retina and predispose to ingrowth of choroidal neovascular membranes, which leak and bleed to cause macular scarring and central visual loss. The same brittleness makes the membrane liable to rupture with subretinal haemorrhage after minor ocular trauma.
additionalDifferentials: Choroidal neovascularisation from age-related macular degeneration
Peripapillary atrophy and other peripapillary changes
additionalInvestigations: Fluorescein angiography to delineate streaks and detect choroidal neovascularisation
Indocyanine green angiography for choroidal detail and neovascular membranes
Optical coherence tomography to identify subretinal fluid, haemorrhage and neovascular membranes
Fundus autofluorescence to highlight the streaks and pigment epithelial changes
Systemic evaluation for pseudoxanthoma elasticum, including skin and cardiovascular assessment
Investigations for associated conditions such as Paget disease of bone and haemoglobinopathies where indicated
redFlags: New distortion, central scotoma or reduced acuity suggesting choroidal neovascularisation
Subretinal haemorrhage, particularly following ocular trauma
Bilateral macular involvement threatening both eyes
Systemic features indicating serious underlying disease such as Paget disease or a haemoglobinopathy
reference.prognosis: The streaks themselves are usually asymptomatic, but the long-term visual prognosis is dictated by choroidal neovascularisation, which commonly affects both eyes over time and can cause substantial central visual loss despite treatment; the risk of trauma-related choroidal rupture persists lifelong.
pitfalls: Diagnosing angioid streaks without investigating for an underlying systemic association
Missing early choroidal neovascularisation because the streaks were assumed to be benign
Failing to counsel patients about the risk of choroidal rupture from minor trauma and the need for eye protection
Confusing angioid streaks with myopic lacquer cracks or traumatic choroidal rupture
Under-monitoring the fellow eye, which is at high risk of neovascular complications
management: Intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy for choroidal neovascularisation, the main treatable threat to central vision
Protective polycarbonate eyewear and avoidance of contact sports to reduce the risk of choroidal rupture from minor trauma
Regular monitoring with optical coherence tomography and home Amsler grid testing for early detection of neovascular membranes
Prompt ophthalmic review of any new distortion or central visual change to enable early treatment
Evaluate and manage the underlying systemic disorder such as pseudoxanthoma elasticum or Paget disease of bone, including cardiovascular assessment
Low-vision rehabilitation and support for patients with established macular scarring
